name: c3-git-at-scale-sample
use_case: Identify the architectural design decisions involved in making Git repositories work at scale, for very many repositories, very large repositories and very many users, on the hosting servers and on the clients, as documented in an engineering article and official engineering background material by the teams that built such systems. For each decision, identify the alternative options the teams adopted or considered and rejected, the forces (quality attributes, constraints and practical concerns) that drive the choice between them, and how decisions relate to one another. Each dimension must name one architectural design decision; its values are the alternative options for that decision.
label: c3-git-at-scale-sample

children.label: Client Repository Performance Strategy
children.description: How client-side Git performance is improved, contrasting integrated configuration and tooling with native Git scalability changes.

children.label: Automatic repository registration
children.description: Newly cloned repositories are automatically registered for recommended configuration and ongoing maintenance.

children.label: Background client maintenance
children.description: Run repository maintenance asynchronously and incrementally so interactive Git commands avoid expensive foreground work.

children.label: Background split commit-graph maintenance
children.description: Reachable commits are maintained asynchronously in incremental split commit-graph layers.

children.label: Complete tracked-path index
children.description: The client index records every tracked path to support core command state inspection.

children.label: Consolidated client maintenance command
children.description: A single foreground command runs the repository maintenance steps together.

children.label: Core Git capability consolidation
children.description: Capabilities formerly supplied by Scalar or management layers are incorporated into core Git, reducing specialized client-layer dependence.

children.label: Custom Git client extensions
children.description: Require a specialized Git client version to deliver repository-scale client performance features.

children.label: Git-integrated filesystem watching
children.description: Git uses a watcher that understands repository semantics such as ignore rules to avoid unnecessary scans.

children.label: Hidden remote-reference namespace
children.description: Fetched remote refs are kept under a hidden namespace for maintenance without changing visible refs.

children.label: Hourly background repository fetch
children.description: Background fetches keep local objects current without placing download work in foreground commands.

children.label: Integrated client optimization configuration
children.description: A managed client setup combines configuration, metadata acceleration, filesystem monitoring, fetching, and background maintenance for large repositories.

children.label: Native Git scalability improvements
children.description: Large-repository performance is improved in Git itself through features such as commit graphs and sparse-checkout enhancements.

children.label: Parallel checkout processing
children.description: Checkout work is processed in parallel to address checkout becoming a bottleneck after virtualization removal.

children.label: Preserved visible branch references during background fetch
children.description: Background fetching updates objects while leaving local and visible remote-tracking branches unchanged.

children.label: Reachability-based commit-graph coverage
children.description: Background graph generation includes every commit reachable through visible and hidden references.

children.label: Repository performance tracing
children.description: Client and repository performance bottlenecks are identified through custom tracing and analysis of user feedback.

children.label: Scalar interim performance layer
children.description: Scalar supplies needed client performance temporarily while equivalent capabilities move into core Git.

children.label: Single-file index stream I/O
children.description: Index data is streamed through one file with cost dominated by sequential file I/O.

children.label: Untracked cache
children.description: Git caches untracked-directory information to reduce large-repository inspection work.

children.label: Updated large-index file format
children.description: An updated index representation reduces I/O and storage for millions of tracked entries.

children.label: Working-directory inspection by core commands
children.description: Core Git commands inspect on-disk working-directory state as part of repository operations.

children.label: Persistent Scalar dependency
children.description: Scalar remains a required long-term layer above Git for repository-scale client performance.

children.label: Virtualized filesystem client
children.description: A virtualized filesystem defers populated-size costs to improve large-repository client performance.

children.label: Foreground garbage collection
children.description: The client periodically performs garbage collection in the foreground during ordinary user work.

children.label: Checkout slowdown after virtualization removal
children.description: Sparse-checkout introduces slower checkout than virtualization because populated-size costs are no longer deferred.

children.label: Compatibility-driven default-off performance features
children.description: Advanced performance features remain disabled by default to preserve broad compatibility.

children.label: Foreground maintenance command blocking
children.description: Synchronous garbage collection delays ordinary interactive Git commands.

children.label: Foreground-fetch overhead
children.description: Generating commit-graph data during foreground fetch adds user-visible fetch work.

children.label: Index compression from 400 MB to 250 MB
children.description: The updated index format reduces the stored index size and corresponding command I/O.

children.label: Low average index-entry processing time
children.description: Large-index commands retain low per-entry processing cost because streaming I/O dominates.

children.label: Multi-million-entry index
children.description: The client supports an index containing more than three million tracked entries.

children.label: Performance decay from deferred cleanup
children.description: Disabling automatic cleanup without effective background maintenance causes object accumulation and gradual performance deterioration.

children.label: System-wide rewrite resource exhaustion
children.description: Large synchronous repository rewrites can consume CPU and memory and stall the entire client system.

children.label: Compaction Maintenance Technique
children.description: Which repacking and object-cleanup techniques maintain compact repository storage?

children.label: Background incremental maintenance
children.description: Repository maintenance runs incrementally in the background rather than blocking interactive operations.

children.label: Loose-object cleanup
children.description: Maintenance removes accumulated loose-object storage to reduce disk and lookup overhead.

children.label: Single-pack full repacking
children.description: Maintenance consolidates all accumulated packfiles into one packfile through a full rewrite.

children.label: Loose-object storage overhead
children.description: Accumulated loose objects consume extra disk space and impose performance costs.

children.label: Pack-count and storage reduction
children.description: Incremental repacking reduces pack-file count, storage footprint, and pack-management pressure.

children.label: Pack-index scan growth
children.description: Accumulating separate pack indexes makes object lookup progressively slower.

children.label: Large-Repository Object Acquisition
children.description: How clients obtain Git data for very large repositories, contrasting complete transfer with demand-driven, server-assisted acquisition.

children.label: GVFS demand-driven transfer
children.description: Initially transfers commits and trees, retrieves missing objects on demand, and can use nearby cache servers to reduce central-server load.

children.label: GVFS-style object-download cache servers
children.description: Separate fetch-object endpoints deliver packfiles while branch-update authority remains on central repository services.

children.label: Partial clone transfer
children.description: Clients use partial clone to reduce large-repository transfer time and local storage when the hosting service supports it.

children.label: GVFS without cache infrastructure
children.description: GVFS deployment proceeds without the cache-server infrastructure required for scalable large-repository access.

children.label: Packfile-based Git networking
children.description: Push and fetch operations transfer Git packfiles over the network.

children.label: Standard-Git GVFS protocol support
children.description: The GVFS protocol is not incorporated into the standard Git client.

children.label: Complete object transfer
children.description: Transfers and verifies the full repository object graph during a conventional clone, creating substantial network, server, client, and latency costs.

children.label: Packfile transfer availability limitation
children.description: Packfile-based transfer and filesystem dependence reduce availability when large storage or servers fail.

children.label: Repository-size threshold for GVFS deployment
children.description: Repository size and user population determine whether GVFS and cache-server infrastructure are warranted.

children.label: Replica State Comparison
children.description: Which checksum or state-comparison technique verifies equivalence between replica contents?

children.label: Checksum-based replica state comparison
children.description: A checksum summarizes logical replica state for equality checking after updates.

children.label: Incremental XOR checksum maintenance
children.description: Reference changes update the logical-state checksum incrementally by removing the old pair hash and adding the new one.

children.label: Full checksum recomputation
children.description: Replica consistency checks recompute the checksum from all references for every update.

children.label: Checksum equality as logical-content equivalence
children.description: Equal replica checksums indicate equivalent logical repository contents.

children.label: Replica Synchronization Mechanism
children.description: Which mechanism distributes or applies repository state across replicas?

children.label: Git-and-rsync replication
children.description: Repository content is replicated using complementary Git and rsync mechanisms.

children.label: Packfile-level application replication
children.description: Git data is replicated at the packfile and reference-transaction layer without distributing the Git implementation itself.

children.label: Git-level distribution
children.description: The architecture distributes or modifies Git itself to provide repository replication.

children.label: Spokes repository replication
children.description: Repository replicas are coordinated through the Spokes architecture to support geographically separated copies.

children.label: DRBD block-level replication
children.description: Repository filesystems are replicated at the block level through DRBD, requiring latency-close replicas.

children.label: Replica Topology
children.description: How many repository replicas are maintained, and what replica-count structure is used?

children.label: Three-replica repository replication
children.description: Each repository maintains a fixed floor of three replicas for consistency, redundancy, and continued push acceptance after one failure.

children.label: Single-extra-copy replication
children.description: Keeps only one additional copy, sufficient for a single-node failure but insufficient for majority-based coordination of concurrent writes.

children.label: Idle-replica resource overhead
children.description: A fixed replica floor consumes substantial resources on numerous small or inactive repositories.

children.label: Replica Write Coordination
children.description: How are replicated repository writes ordered, committed, and accepted?

children.label: Consensus-free write acceptance
children.description: Any repository instance may accept writes, using storage-level atomic updates instead of elected consensus primaries.

children.label: Consistency-and-partition-tolerance priority
children.description: Replica write coordination prioritizes consistency and partition tolerance over write availability.

children.label: Durability-gated write acceptance
children.description: Writes are accepted only after the required number of replicas have synchronously committed them.

children.label: Orchestrated push fan-out
children.description: An orchestrator distributes pushed packfiles and reference transactions to repository instances.

children.label: Overlapped replica-coordination work
children.description: The coordinator performs database, checksum, and lock work concurrently while replica communication is in flight.

children.label: Per-write voting without a primary
children.description: Each write directly determines its winning order and outcome rather than following a primary's global ordering.

children.label: Read-preserving replicated-write optimization
children.description: Replication write acceleration is designed without degrading the much more frequent repository reads.

children.label: Replica-based distributed locking
children.description: Replicas provide distributed locks that order coordinated database updates.

children.label: Rollback of non-majority writes
children.description: Writes failing majority agreement are reverted where applied to preserve surviving replica agreement.

children.label: Single-local-repository synchronization
children.description: Reference transactions synchronize with one local repository rather than a replica quorum.

children.label: Strict-majority coordinated writes
children.description: Uses three replicas, majority-held exclusive locks, strict-majority acceptance, and replica-wide serialization to prevent conflicting divergent writes.

children.label: Three-phase commit coordination
children.description: Replicas synchronize reference updates through coordinator-directed prepare, commit, and rollback phases.

children.label: Transactional Git reference updates
children.description: Git reference mutations use atomic, validated transactions that produce deterministic results and roll back completely on failure.

children.label: Unsynchronized packfile distribution
children.description: Pushed packfiles fan out without consensus because they are unreachable until references commit.

children.label: Reference-update amplification
children.description: Pull-request bookkeeping can multiply one user push into many additional replicated reference updates.

children.label: Replica round-trip coordination latency
children.description: Multiple distant-replica round trips consume the write-coordination latency budget.

children.label: Replica-count push-throughput degradation
children.description: Adding replicas reduces push throughput because consensus waits on more participants and their tail latency.

children.label: Replica-distance reference-update limit
children.description: Geographic replica latency bounds sustainable per-repository reference-update throughput.

children.label: Slowest-replica consensus latency
children.description: Coordinated replication latency is bounded by the slowest participating replica.

children.label: Write unavailability during replication shortfall
children.description: Writes become temporarily unavailable when the required replica count cannot be synchronously achieved.

children.label: Repository Placement and Read Routing
children.description: How are repositories placed and requests routed to suitable hosting replicas?

children.label: Closest sufficiently fresh replica routing
children.description: Reads route to the geographically closest replica that meets freshness requirements.

children.label: Explicit repository-location tracking
children.description: An external routing table records the machines holding each repository copy and supports locating and validating those copies.

children.label: Rendezvous-hashed repository routing
children.description: Repository IDs are mapped to expected healthy servers using rendezvous hashing, with placement adjusted as membership changes.

children.label: Single-replica read routing
children.description: After synchronized publication, each fetch or clone is routed to one repository replica rather than coordinated reads across replicas.

children.label: Stale-routing recovery
children.description: Routing may be stale after failures, and the system restores service by materializing repository state on a newly selected server.

children.label: Stateless repository placement
children.description: Any healthy server can materialize repository state without authoritative per-repository placement records.

children.label: External routing-database placement
children.description: Depend on an external routing database to locate repositories across hosting servers.

children.label: Per-server repository location tracking
children.description: The system tracks repository placement on every server as authoritative routing state.

children.label: Single on-disk repository behind HTTP
children.description: An HTTP frontend serves one conventional on-disk repository from a single host.
